source.title: Picking Winning Tickets Before Training by Preserving Gradient Flow
source.authors: Chaoqi Wang; Chao-Qi Wang; Guodong Zhang; R. Grosse

record.tranche_reason: The paper trains sparse subnetworks found before training and reports their training loss, directly bearing on underfitting and optimization, but it does not test the versions' claims about dense networks reaching zero classification error.
record.gate_note: The paper reports training-loss curves for pruned ResNet32 on CIFAR-100 at 98% pruning, comparing GraSP and SNIP. Other accuracy tables report test accuracy and do not establish training classification error. Comparisons cited from prior work are not rows.
record.test_reason: GraSP uses the premise that preserving gradient flow helps optimization to design a pruning criterion. Its results compare pruning methods, without measuring any version's specified effect: training classification error, spurious minima, depth degradation, initialization-dependent training speed or depth, learning-rate stability, or batch-normalization benefits.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors propose pruning at initialization by preserving gradient flow, report competitive test accuracy and advantages over SNIP at high sparsity, and identify underfitting as the main bottleneck in their convergence experiment. They acknowledge a remaining performance gap relative to pruning trained networks and better lottery-ticket performance with late resetting.
record.recipe_differences: The study prunes at initialization using a gradient-flow-preservation criterion, then trains the resulting sparse network. The claim versions concern dense-network training, local minima, depth, initialization, learning-rate stability, or batch normalization.
record.method_sensitivity: Pruning method (GraSP versus SNIP) changes the plotted training-loss trajectory in the CIFAR-100, ResNet32, 98%-pruning comparison. The paper also reports initialization and batch-size variation for test accuracy, outside the claim versions' specified outcomes.

fits_no_version.finding: For CIFAR-100 with doubled-filter ResNet32 at 98% pruning, GraSP produces lower training loss and faster loss reduction than SNIP (Section 5.2, Figure 1).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Preserving gradient flow when pruning at initialization can improve subsequent training-loss trajectories relative to connection-sensitivity pruning at extreme sparsity.

record.problems: The relevant training-loss results appear only in a figure, with no numeric values stated in the text. The comparison concerns pruned networks and reports loss rather than training classification error. The paper says it runs each CIFAR experiment for 3 trials, and reports 10 trials for initialization gradient-norm analyses, but the plotted training-loss uncertainty is not specified in the text.
record.rows_left_out: Test-accuracy tables for pruned models, initialization/batch-size test-accuracy ablations, gradient-norm measurements, and layerwise sparsity plots were not extracted because they do not measure training classification error or another outcome named by the claim versions. Prior-work results discussed or cited are not this study's own results.

untested.parts: Zero or near-zero training classification error, including random labels, and its dependence on model size, stopping time or regularization. Sparse-network training loss does not establish these outcomes.
Spurious local minima and the effect of extra student neurons in two-layer ReLU teacher-student problems.
Training-error degradation across plain-network depths and its prevention by identity shortcuts or special initialization.
Initialization-dependent training speed and trainable depth, including orthogonal versus Gaussian weights. Table 5 measures test accuracy of pruned residual networks.
Loss recovery, curvature changes, divergence and edge-of-stability dynamics relative to learning-rate stability thresholds.
Training speed and learning-rate tolerance with versus without batch normalization, including Fixup.

record.verdict_notes: The record's tests/T2 classification conflicts with its correctly unlinked rows. The initialization ablation and gradient-norm measurements do not test V4's training-speed or trainable-depth outcomes. Results attributed to earlier studies are not this paper's own evidence.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test zero or near-zero training classification error for sufficiently large convolutional networks, corrupted or random labels, or the effects of size and training duration.
No two-layer ReLU teacher-student experiments or width sweep.
Does not compare plain networks with identity shortcuts across depths.
Does not test initialization effects on plain-network training speed or trainable depth; initialization ablation reports test accuracy of pruned ResNet32, not the version's named outcomes.
No learning-rate stability or sharpness experiments.

rows.subject: ResNet32
rows.stage_stated: trained from initialization after GraSP pruning
rows.operation_detail: Train the 98%-pruned subnetwork obtained with GraSP; plot training loss over epochs.
rows.baseline: SNIP-pruned ResNet32, plotted separately; numeric baseline not stated
rows.note: The text says GraSP achieves much lower training loss and its decrease is faster than SNIP; precise values are only plotted. The measure is loss, not training classification error, so it does not map to a claim version.
rows.check: This is the study's own pruning method compared with SNIP, rather than a result on a claim version. Lower and faster-decreasing training loss is explicitly reported, but does not establish near-zero training classification error. The subject should specify ResNet32 with twice the usual filters per convolutional layer (Section 5.1 footnote).

rows.subject: ResNet32
rows.stage_stated: trained from initialization after SNIP pruning
rows.operation_detail: Train the 98%-pruned subnetwork obtained with SNIP; plot training loss over epochs.
rows.baseline: GraSP-pruned ResNet32, plotted separately; numeric baseline not stated
rows.note: The text says SNIP's training loss is higher and decreases more slowly than GraSP's. Precise values are only plotted; loss does not measure training classification error.
rows.check: This is the comparator in a pruning-method evaluation, rather than a result on a claim version. Higher and slower-decreasing training loss does not establish a training classification-error rate. The subject should specify ResNet32 with twice the usual filters per convolutional layer (Section 5.1 footnote).
